title: GPX Heart Rate Analyzer: Zones From Your File
description: Analyse heart rate recorded in a GPX file with the GPX Heart Rate Analyzer — average, maximum and time in zones, read locally. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, against an estimated maximum of 190 bpm (the 220-minus-age estimate at 30), the common zone boundaries fall at 114, 133, 152 and 171 bpm — and the analyzer prices how long you actually spent beyond each.
quick_answer: The GPX Heart Rate Analyzer reads the heart-rate channel hidden in a GPX file's extensions and reports average, maximum and time-in-zone estimates from the recording itself. Drop the file — it is read locally, never uploaded — and see the effort story your map viewers have been ignoring.

Apps disagree about zone boundaries and smoothing. The file's own samples are the raw material every one of them started from — start there too.
Heart data is intimate. An analyzer that runs locally, on the file you drop, keeps the reading between you and your browser.
A strap that died at kilometre 12 shows as heart data that simply stops — the analyzer's coverage makes dropouts visible instead of averaging over them silently.

Heart rate rides inside GPX extensions — typically Garmin's TrackPointExtension, where each trackpoint can carry an <hr> value beside its <ele> and <time>. Files from phones without a strap or sensor simply have no channel to analyse.

An average of 148 bpm over a hilly run hides everything interesting: the zones show whether that was steady threshold work or a sawtooth of climbs and recoveries averaging out to the same innocent number.

popular_table.title: The common five-zone model
popular_table.intro: Zones as percentage bands of maximum heart rate — the model most tools start from (boundaries computed for a 190 bpm maximum).
popular_table.note: Maximum heart rate here uses the 220 − age estimate (190 at age 30), which errs by ±10 bpm or more for individuals. Zone conclusions are estimates with that uncertainty baked in — physiology, not surveying.

faq: Recordings from watches and bike computers paired with a chest strap or optical sensor — written by Garmin, Wahoo, Suunto, Polar and others into GPX extensions. A phone-only recording usually has no HR channel.
What does 'time in zone' weigh by?
By the recording's own samples — each trackpoint's heart rate counts for the time until the next point. Dense recordings price zones more faithfully than sparse ones.

Almost certainly a sensor artefact (strap slip, cadence lock, a dry-contact spike at the start). Optical and strap sensors both produce a few wild samples; a single spike does not move the average much, but it owns the 'maximum' line unless filtered.

An optical sensor mistaking your step rhythm for your pulse, reporting ~170–180 (running cadence) as heart rate. It produces suspiciously steady high readings early in runs before sweat improves contact.
Not honestly from heart rate alone — calorie models need body mass, age, sex and device-specific coefficients the file does not carry. This analyzer reports what the recording actually contains.
Zone percentages need a maximum; the 220 − age estimate is the common default. A lab-tested or field-tested personal maximum makes every zone truer.
